Libya Imposes Sweeping Import Ban, Disrupting Trade and Key Industries

TRIPOLI, June 19—Libya’s Government of National Stability on Wednesday enforced a sweeping ban on imports of non-essential goods, a move officials say is aimed at conserving foreign currency reserves amid a deteriorating balance of payments. The measure, which took effect overnight, has brought commercial activity at major ports to a standstill and left manufacturers and retailers scrambling to secure supplies.

The ban covers a wide range of consumer products, machinery, and industrial inputs, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Economy. Only basic foodstuffs, medicines, and fuel are exempt. Authorities say the restrictions will remain in place “until further notice.”

The decision is already impacting several of Libya’s largest companies, including National Oil Corp, which relies on imported equipment and spare parts to maintain production at its oil fields. “Our supply chain has been severely disrupted,” a National Oil Corp spokesperson said. “We are working with the government to seek exemptions for critical items needed to ensure continued operations.”

Traders at Tripoli port report dozens of cargo containers stranded on the docks. “We have shipments from Europe and Asia waiting for clearance,” said Hatem al-Saadi, a customs broker. “Importers are confused, and many are worried about shortages in the coming weeks.”

The Libyan Importers’ Union estimates that over $1.8 billion worth of goods could be affected monthly if the ban continues. “This will have immediate consequences for employment and prices,” said union head Salem Dabbashi. “Retailers are facing gaps on their shelves already.”

Economists warn the restrictions risk stoking inflation and further weakening Libya’s fragile economy. “Libya depends heavily on imports, not just for finished products but also for inputs to industry, agriculture, and infrastructure,” said Amal Farjani, an economist at the University of Tripoli. “A prolonged embargo could hit growth and may even affect oil exports if supplies to the sector are disrupted.”

Some business owners, however, voiced cautious support for the government’s move. “We understand the need to stabilize the currency,” said Fathi Ghariani, owner of a Benghazi-based construction firm. “But there must be clear guidelines and a timeline.”

The government has promised to review requests for exemptions and urged companies to submit documentation for critical imports. Meanwhile, as the ban enters its second day, Libyans are bracing for price hikes and possible shortages as the country’s supply chains adjust to the new reality.
